segs.text: Section twenty nine. Medication misadventures. Three overlapping terms describe drug related problems. An adverse drug event is an injury related to a drug, preventable or not. A medication error is a preventable mistake anywhere in the medication process, whether or not anyone is hurt. An adverse drug reaction is a harmful effect of a drug given at the right dose. All three are kinds of medication misadventures, the broadest term. Adverse drug reactions lie wholly within adverse drug events, and medication errors overlap both: an adverse drug reaction is always an adverse drug event and can also be a medication error, while an error that injures no one is not an adverse drug event.

The Institute of Medicine defines the adverse drug event, and the key word is injury, from preventable or non preventable causes. It can happen even when the correct drug was prescribed and given, for example in a patient whose genetic background gives an unwanted effect from a drug people are not normally genotyped for. A wrong dose written but never harming anyone is only a medication error; given and causing injury, it becomes a preventable adverse drug event.

The National Coordinating Council for Medication Error Reporting and Prevention defines a medication error as any preventable event that may cause inappropriate medication use or patient harm while the medication is in the control of the healthcare professional, patient, or consumer. So a patient can make one at home, and the outcome does not matter. Errors are prevented by fixing the process: clear documentation of orders, separating drugs with similar sounding names, since stock is often stored alphabetically, and distinct labeling and separate storage for high concentration insulin. Errors are reported to the Institute for Safe Medication Practices reporting program, including an error that is about to happen but has not happened yet. Stop that error first, for example through a supervisor, then report it.

The World Health Organization defines an adverse drug reaction as any noxious, unintended, and undesired effect of a drug at doses used for prophylaxis, diagnosis, or therapy, implying a causal link to the drug. The key words are right dose: the drug itself causes the harm, not the amount. The other adverse drug events involve too little drug, stopping a drug, too much drug, or a mistake. Adverse drug reactions are reported through the F D A MedWatch program, not the medication error program.

Adverse drug events fall into five types: therapeutic failure, withdrawal events, overdose, medication error, and adverse drug reaction. Therapeutic failure is too little drug, and nonadherence is probably the biggest reason. Withdrawal events follow stopping a long term drug such as opioids, hypertension medications, or S S R I drugs. Accidental overdoses occur most in children and older adults, because both have a different kinetic profile, and older patients may forget doses they already took; children most often overdose on iron tablets that look like candy. Intentional overdoses are mostly young adults to adults.

Institutions also watch for adverse drug reactions, an important public health concern. Those compliant with the accrediting body J C A H O must define significant reactions, start intensive assessments for reactions that meet that definition. They must also follow up on the causes, such as a dosing issue or pharmacogenomics that should have been used and was missed. A sentinel event, a risk of death or serious physical or psychological injury, may trigger an unscheduled J C A H O visit and process reviews.
